title: Dry firewood without a meter: split, stack, cover, and know when it's ready
summary: Split wood dries; whole rounds hardly do. Split it, stack it off the ground in sun and wind, cover only the top, and give softwood a summer and hardwood one to two years, then check the ends, weight, sound and a fresh split before you burn it. Wet wood gives little heat and coats the chimney with creosote, and dead standing trees drop limbs and tops without warning.

materials.item: Rounds or logs cut about 25 mm (1 in) shorter than the firebox, 400 mm (16 in) on many stoves
Axe or splitting maul, steel wedges and a sledge (see Axe care)
Rails, poles or heat-treated (HT) pallets to keep the stack off the ground
Roofing metal, plywood or a tarp for the top of the stack only

steps.text: Plan a year ahead. Hardwood needs one to two years to dry and softwood about a summer (Drolet Part 1, CMHC wood heat), so the wood you cut this winter is next winter's heat. Cut by early spring at the latest (NRCan wood heating).
Collect from the ground first: fallen trees, broken limbs and blowdown. Look up before you stand under any tree, dead or alive.
steps.warn: Dead trees and broken tops fall without warning. Keep two tree lengths from a snag you aren't felling (OSHA eTool hazards); clearing bent or hung-up trees is its own card.

steps.text: Cut to length: about 25 mm (1 in) shorter than your firebox, 400 mm (16 in) on many stoves (Drolet Part 1).
steps.warn: Chainsaw work: leg protection, hard hat, eye and face protection, hearing protection, work gloves and protective boots, and never alone (OSHA chainsaws). See Clearing a fallen tree for the full kit.

steps.text: Split every round as soon as you can, to pieces 75 to 150 mm (3 to 6 in) across (Drolet Part 1). Unsplit rounds can stay wet for over a year (UMD FS-1074).
steps.warn: Axe and maul: eye protection, hard hat, gloves and steel-toe boots, a sturdy block on level ground, children kept out of range, and stop when tired (BC Forest Safety Council). Check the head is tight first (see Axe care).

steps.text: Pick a spot in sun and wind, and lay rails, poles or heat-treated (HT) pallets so the stack sits off the ground (NRCan wood heating, UMD FS-1074).
Stack the pieces split side down in rows with gaps between the rows, so air moves under and through (EPA Burn Wise efficiency, NRCan wood heating).
Cover the top only, with roofing metal, plywood or a tarp tied over the top. Leave the sides open (EPA Burn Wise, Penn State heating).

Before burning, check several signs: cracked ends, ends gone grey or yellow, a hollow knock, light weight, and a fresh split that feels warm and dry, not cool and damp (CMHC wood heat, Drolet Part 1).
If you have a moisture meter, split a piece that has warmed indoors and push the pins into the middle of the fresh face. Burn it at 20 % or less (EPA Burn Wise, UMD FS-1074, FPL meters).
Bring two or three days' wood inside to warm up (NRCan wood heating), stacked outside the stove's clearances (Drolet Part 1).
steps.warn: A big pile of wet wood indoors breeds mould (NRCan wood heating).

steps.text: If wet wood is all you have, split it small and add a few pieces at a time to a hot fire of dry wood (our own reasoning: Drolet lists unseasoned wood as a fuel not to burn, and UGA says evaporating water cools the fire and favours creosote). Turn the air down only once it flames brightly (Drolet Part 1).
steps.warn: Never choke a wet load to a smoulder: it coats the chimney with creosote and makes carbon monoxide. Check the pipe and chimney more often than every two months (Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: Keep a tally of how fast the pile goes in a cold week, and cut more than you think you need (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat).

notes:
## Why dry wood matters
Fresh-cut wood is 35 to 60 % water by weight (NRCan wood heating). Wood that wet is hard to light, hisses and smokes, and spends much of its heat boiling off the water, so you burn more wood for less warmth (NRCan wood heating, UMD FS-1074). The smoke that doesn't burn settles in the pipe as soot and creosote, the fuel of chimney fires (UMD FS-1074). When a stove smokes or won't heat, check the wood first: wet wood is the most common problem with wood heat (NRCan wood heating).

## Split, stack, cover
- **Split everything.** Whole rounds hardly dry. In a Maryland trial, hickory left in unsplit rounds 40 to 45 cm (16 to 18 in) long was still over 30 % moisture after a year; split pieces reached about 20 % in six months (UMD FS-1074). Split to a range of sizes from about 75 to 150 mm (3 to 6 in) across (Drolet Part 1).
- **Cut to length** about 25 mm (1 in) shorter than the firebox; 400 mm (16 in) is the common length (Drolet Part 1).
- **Splitting and lifting hurt people.** Chopping wood risks cuts, lost fingers and strains of the shoulder, arm and wrist (BC Forest Safety Council). Wear eye protection, a hard hat, gloves and steel-toe boots, split on a sturdy block on level ground, keep children well out of range, and stop when you are tired (BC Forest Safety Council). Drive a wedge with a sledge whose face is larger than the wedge's, never strike one maul with another, and throw out any maul or wedge that is dented, cracked, chipped or mushroomed (Council right tool). Struck steel can shed splinters: see the [projectile card](#browse/hazards/projectile) and [Axe care](#guides/skill_axe_care).
- **Stack it in sun and wind,** off the ground on rails, poles or pallets, with gaps so air moves under and through the pile (NRCan wood heating, UMD FS-1074). Split side down (EPA Burn Wise efficiency).
- **Cover the top only.** Roofing metal or plywood over the top sheds rain and snow; a tarp pulled down the sides holds the damp in (EPA Burn Wise, Penn State heating). A woodshed works if air moves through it (UMD FS-1074), though Drolet finds wood dries faster in the open (Drolet Part 1).
- **Start early.** Trees cut in late summer, fall or winter hold less sap than spring-cut ones (UMD FS-1074), and wood cut and split by early spring dries over the summer (NRCan wood heating). Wood that someone else cut is rarely dry; plan to dry it yourself (Drolet Part 1).

## How long it takes
| Wood (split, stacked, top covered) | Time | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Softwood (pine, spruce, poplar, aspen) split small | One summer | Drolet Part 1, CMHC wood heat |
| Any softwood | At least 6 months | EPA Burn Wise efficiency |
| Hardwood (oak, maple, ash) | One to two years; longer for big pieces | Drolet Part 1, CMHC wood heat |
| Any hardwood | At least 12 months | EPA Burn Wise efficiency |
| Black cherry, hackberry (Maryland trial, uncovered) | About 7 months | UMD FS-1074 |
| Hickory, black locust (same trial) | Hickory about 24 % on average, black locust about 26 % inside, after a year | UMD FS-1074 |

Oak wasn't in the Maryland trial; its author expects it to dry like hickory or black locust. Maryland is warmer than most of Canada, and the same author says drying takes longer in northern and humid places (UMD FS-1074); Drolet says the same of damp climates and of winter (Drolet Part 1). Wood left lying in a swamp, or cut more than about three years ago, tends to be rotten and burns badly (NRCan wood heating).

### Which wood gives the most heat
A kilogram of dry wood gives about the same heat whatever the species; what differs is density, so a cord of hardwood holds much more heat than a cord of softwood (NRCan wood heating). NRCan ranks common Canadian firewoods from hardest to softest: ironwood, rock elm, hickory, oak, sugar maple, beech, yellow birch, ash, red elm, red maple, tamarack, Douglas fir, white birch, Manitoba maple, red alder, hemlock, poplar, pine, basswood, spruce, balsam (NRCan wood heating). Burn the softwood in spring and fall and save the hardwood for the cold (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1).

## Is it ready?
| Check | Dry | Still wet | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ends | Cracks (checks) across the end grain | No cracks | NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat, Penn State heating |
| Colour | Ends gone from white or cream to grey or yellow | Bright, fresh | CMHC wood heat, Drolet Part 1 |
| Weight | Much lighter | Heavy for its size | NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1 |
| Knock two pieces | Hollow sound | Dull thud | CMHC wood heat, EPA Burn Wise |
| Split one and feel the new face | Warm and dry | Cool and damp | CMHC wood heat, Drolet Part 1 |
| On the fire | Catches and flames | Hisses and sizzles | CMHC wood heat |

Use several signs together. The ends dry first: in the Maryland trial the wood near the ends dried well ahead of the middle (UMD FS-1074), so cracked ends can hide a wet core. Loose bark is not one of the signs these sources give, so don't lean on it.

## A moisture meter, if one turns up
Pin-type wood moisture meters are sold at hardware and home stores and woodstove shops (UMD FS-1074, NRCan wood heating). Some cheap ones show coloured lights for a range instead of a number (UMD FS-1074).
- Split a piece and push the pins into the middle of the fresh face, not the end (UMD FS-1074).
- Ready: 20 % or less (EPA Burn Wise). Drolet aims for 15 to 20 % (Drolet Part 1). Over 30 % isn't seasoned at all (UMD FS-1074).
- Readings shift with the wood's temperature and species (FPL meters), so test a piece that has warmed indoors and treat the number as a guide.

## When wet wood is all you have
- Split it small and bring in two or three days' worth to warm up (NRCan wood heating), stacked outside the stove's clearances (Drolet Part 1; see [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install)). Don't store a big pile of wet wood indoors: it breeds mould (NRCan wood heating).
- Add it a few pieces at a time to a hot fire of dry wood. No maker or agency sets a rule for mixing, and Drolet lists unseasoned wood among the fuels not to burn (Drolet Part 1). UGA says evaporating water cools the burn and favours creosote (UGA seasoned wood), so keep the wet pieces a small share of a hot fire; that is our own reasoning, not a tested rule.
- Turn the air down only once the load burns brightly. If the flames die when you close the air, the wood is too wet (Drolet Part 1). Glass that stains dark quickly means the fire is too low or the wood too wet (NRCan wood heating).
- Never choke it to a smoulder: that builds creosote and makes carbon monoxide (see [Get through winter in one heated room](#guides/skill_staying_warm) and [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)).
- Check the pipe and chimney more often. Drolet says at least every two months of the heating season with good wood (Drolet Part 1); with wet wood, check sooner. See [Sweeping a chimney](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping) and [Check a chimney](#guides/test_chimney).

## Dead trees: free fuel that falls on people
Standing dead wood burns best (TC 21-3), which is why people go for it. It is also how firewood cutters get hurt:
- Dead trees and broken tops come down without warning. OSHA tells loggers to bring a dead or broken standing tree (a snag) down with a machine, or keep two tree lengths away (OSHA eTool hazards). Cut a dead tree and the top can break off (OSHA trim).
- Ash killed by the emerald ash borer goes brittle fast. Big limbs can snap 9 m (30 ft) up on a calm day, and Purdue's advice for a dead tree that can't be felled is to stay away from it until it falls (Purdue ash).
- Penn State advises against cutting snags for firewood: they can be very difficult to fell (Penn State heating).

Take what is already on the ground first, look up before you stand under anything, and read [Clearing a fallen tree](#guides/safety_clearing_blowdown) before cutting anything bent or hung up. Check what you are about to burn in [What to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn).

## How much a winter takes
- A full cord is a stack 1.2 x 1.2 x 2.4 m (4 x 4 x 8 ft), 3.62 cubic metres of wood and air. A face cord or stove cord is one row of short pieces: three face cords of 40 cm (16 in) pieces make one full cord (NRCan wood heating).
- NRCan's 2002 guide: a medium-sized modern house heated only with wood uses 3 to 5 full cords a winter, or 1 to 2 with a high-efficiency stove in the main living area (NRCan wood heating). CMHC's 2008 edition says 2 to 4 full cords for wood-only heat, and 1 to 2 when the stove carries part of the load (CMHC wood heat).
- Both say more for very cold places, big, leaky or poorly insulated houses, and softwood, and that only experience tells (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat).
- Both guides give whole-house figures, not figures for one heated room; that depends on the climate, the stove and how tight the room is. Keep a tally. Note how long a stacked row lasts in a cold week and multiply by the weeks of winter left. Cut more than you think: dry wood stored well keeps more than a year (NRCan wood heating).
